title: Social Psychology

jokes.text: Professor announces anonymous evaluations were so harsh he 'took the time personally to analyze the handwriting against past exams'
jokes.setup: Professor announces he valued the anonymous, constructive feedback from students
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he deanonymized the cards by analyzing handwriting — the opposite of accepting anonymous criticism gracefully
jokes.explanation: Chang's escalating pettiness is perfectly in character — the reveal that he undermined the anonymity of anonymous evaluations is a great inversion. Character-specific: only Chang would do this. The structure is clean: the setup establishes normalcy, the punchline obliterates it.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: I received some rather harsh feedback on my evaluation cards. So I did what any reasonable academic would do—I performed a full CSI-level handwriting analysis to identify the anonymous critic.

jokes.text: 'De nada.' / 'You don't have to sign your name anymore.' / 'Got it.'
jokes.setup: Professor says 'gracias' at the end of his thanks
jokes.punchline: A student reflexively responds 'De nada,' and the professor has to remind students the evaluations are anonymous — implying the student just incriminated themselves
jokes.explanation: Four words do enormous comedic work. The student's reflexive 'De nada' paired with the professor's calm reminder ('you don't have to sign your name') is a brilliantly economical bit — the student has accidentally revealed themselves without saying anything incriminating. 'Got it' as the final beat is perfect understatement. This is tight, smart writing.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: You see, when analyzing handwriting, one must pay close attention to every minute detail. For instance, the way one dots their i's and crosses their t's reveals much about a person's character.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: *mockingly demonstrates dotting motions with exaggerated sound effects* Psh-psh-psh. Oh yes, very telling. A person who dots their i's with such careless abandon clearly has authority issues and probable substance abuse problems.

jokes.text: Chang specifies the eval was 'racist' in a list with 'harsh and hurtful' — delivered as a casual add-on
jokes.setup: Chang says the evaluation was 'so harsh and hurtful'
jokes.punchline: He adds 'and racist' as an afterthought, as if that's a minor detail
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the word placement — 'racist' dropped in deadpan after 'harsh and hurtful' as a subordinate clause. The understatement through structure rather than tone is sharp writing. Economy is near-perfect: one word doing huge comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Who's unstable? Who's unstable? I'm perfectly stable! I have a very orderly life. I wake up, I evaluate people, I go to bed. That's stability. That's discipline. That's the mark of a well-adjusted individual. So don't you dare suggest that I'm unstable just because I occasionally raise my voice or organize my files by the molecular weight of their contents or spend fourteen hours recalibrating my grading scale because I detected a 0.003% variance in my assessment methodology. I am the picture of mental health! So I ask you: who here is unstable? Who?

jokes.text: Chang describes the culprit dots her i's with 'tiny, itty-bitty, little circles' and mimes them going 'Boop. Boop. Tcch!'
jokes.setup: Chang is trying to expose the anonymous student through forensic detail
jokes.punchline: His performance devolves into mimicking the cute circles with onomatopoeia — revealing unhinged pettiness dressed as serious investigation
jokes.explanation: The physical specificity of 'Boop. Boop. Tcch!' transforms a cold-blooded act of vindictiveness into absurdist comedy. The rhythm of the three sounds is well-constructed. Only Chang performs like this in a serious moment of grievance.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't forget anything. I strategically time my exits to avoid awkward small talk.

jokes.text: Chang says 'Who's erratic and unstable now, Princess Gringa?' then blows a kiss at the student
jokes.setup: The student called Chang 'erratic and unstable' in the evaluation
jokes.punchline: Chang's entire unhinged performance proves the student's evaluation correct — and 'Princess Gringa' as the condescending nickname is the topper
jokes.explanation: Perfect irony: by trying to prove he's NOT erratic and unstable, Chang proves he absolutely is. 'Princess Gringa' as the nickname is a great invention — condescending, specific, and a little racist (tying back to joke 2). The kiss-off (literal) is a terrific button. This is among the episode's best gags — a complete comedic argument in one line.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, small talk is like a marathon. You can't just sprint out of the gate. You pace yourself, conserve energy, and then when you see your opening, you make your move.

jokes.text: Jeff says he forgot to 'stagger the timing of his exit with Shirley's' to avoid the long walk with her
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta are walking out of class together
jokes.punchline: Jeff's real concern is that he strategically times exits to avoid being stuck in prolonged small talk with Shirley
jokes.explanation: Funny social observation that reveals Jeff's self-absorbed calculation. The idea of deliberately 'staggering your exit' to avoid a conversation is a very specific and relatable anxiety elevated by Jeff's clinical framing. Character-specific to Jeff's detached social engineering.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Your conversational abilities aren't as sharp as you think they are.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh please, my wit is like track and field — it's fast, it's competitive, and I always finish strong.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: More like the long jump — lots of buildup, but you never quite stick the landing.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm a sprinter. I'm at my best during high-speed bursts of wit. On a Shirley walk I'd be winded by that stoner tree.'
jokes.setup: Britta defends Shirley as easy to talk to and notes Jeff has 'an Olympic gold medal in jibber-jabber'
jokes.punchline: Jeff reframes his conversational shortcoming as an athletic specialty — he's a 'sprinter' not a marathon talker — and the 'stoner tree' as a geographic landmark is a perfect specific detail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Jeff spinning his social shallowness as an athletic metaphor ('sprinter,' 'winded') is clever self-justification. The specificity of 'that stoner tree' as a recognizable campus landmark anchors the abstraction in comedy-college reality. Economical and very quotable. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — well-constructed, character-specific, highly repeatable.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: No worries.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No worries? Dude, hacky sack expired culturally in 1987. You're like three decades too late to the party.

jokes.text: Britta encounters Vaughn and Jeff immediately says: 'Interesting. 'Cause I might be worried if I was playing hacky sack a decade too late.'
jokes.setup: Vaughn cheerfully says 'No worries' when greeting Britta
jokes.punchline: Jeff weaponizes Vaughn's 'no worries' to mock his outdated hacky sack hobby — a quick, cutting dismissal
jokes.explanation: Economical snark. The pivot from Vaughn's 'no worries' to 'you might be worried if...' is a nice structural inversion. 'A decade too late' is a good specific dig. Classic Jeff mode: belittling with precision.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I can have normal conversations. I'm very normal. See? I'm talking to you right now about regular things.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That was a successful social interaction. I'd rate it at about 7.3 millimeters of normal.

jokes.text: Jeff claims he and Britta walked '100 yards with no awkward pauses — that's the sign of a true friend.' Britta responds: 'I'm really glad you're not hitting on me anymore.'
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a sincere-sounding observation about their friendship progress, framing it as evidence of genuine connection
jokes.punchline: Britta completely reframes it — his 'friendship' is just a failed pursuit, and her relief at him stopping is the real truth of their dynamic
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant — Jeff sets up a sincere-seeming beat about friendship, Britta deflates it perfectly by revealing what she's actually thinking. The punchline works because it's simultaneously an insult and a compliment (she's glad the pressure is off, implying progress of a kind). Character-specific: only Britta would say this so bluntly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're good friends, Britta. I can prove it.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Name one time I've ever made things awkward between us.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That.

jokes.text: Beat: Jeff says 'There's the awkward pause' immediately after Britta's line, then walks away to an audible reaction
jokes.setup: Jeff just declared no awkward pauses = true friendship
jokes.punchline: Britta's rebuke creates exactly the awkward pause he claimed they'd transcended — Jeff dryly names it
jokes.explanation: A fast, clean callback that immediately pays off Jeff's earlier setup. The self-awareness of naming it is very Jeff. Economy is nearly perfect — three words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, I walked into that one.

jokes.text: Annie explains she lost her scholarship AND virginity due to the pills that were supposed to help her focus
jokes.setup: Annie is pitching herself for the psych lab by explaining her academic credentials and why she's at community college
jokes.punchline: The list escalates unexpectedly: lost scholarship (bad) → lost virginity (shocking addition delivered flatly as equivalent damage)
jokes.explanation: The escalation from academic failure to sexual misfortune — delivered in the same clinical, over-sharing register — is a great character joke. It's very Annie: TMI sincerity used as a persuasion strategy. The flat delivery of such a personal detail as equivalent to a scholarship loss is perfectly cringe-funny.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Professor Duncan, I just wanted to show you my extra credit essay on comparative literature. I stayed up all night researching. Also, I've won three academic awards this semester. And I'm fluent in Spanish, Mandarin, and conversational French. Oh, and I'm a member of the National Honor Society.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: My father never believed in me, so I've been trying to prove myself my whole life. I have trust issues. I bite my nails when I'm anxious, which is always. I once cried in a Bed Bath & Beyond because they were out of my preferred thread count. I'm terrified of disappointing people, which is why I'm here at 2 AM with this essay.

jokes.text: Professor Duncan says 'I'm not allowed to date students — even though you're an eight. Which is a British ten, so I'm angry.'
jokes.setup: Annie expects a professional response to her academic pitch; Duncan prepares to 'be upfront'
jokes.punchline: His upfrontness is entirely about attraction — 'not allowed to date students' followed by rating her and expressing personal grievance about the rule
jokes.explanation: The 'British ten' explanation is an unexpected and funny bit of logic — the exchange rate on attractiveness scales. The structure is tight: rules → rating → nationalistic grievance. The last beat ('so I'm angry') is a perfect absurdist topper. Very quotable. Earns its high scores through tight construction.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Oh, Annie. I'm flattered, but I'm afraid I must decline. You see, in Britain, we have standards.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: A PG rating here means something entirely different than in America. What you're suggesting would be at least a 15 certificate.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Besides, you're a student, and I'm a professor. That's simply not done across the pond.

jokes.text: Duncan offers Annie a spot in the lab 'if you could lend me a fiver' and explains he left his 'purse in my duffle and my duffle in the boot of my lorry'
jokes.setup: Duncan has just said Annie can join the lab despite the age restriction
jokes.punchline: He immediately asks for money, deploying maximum British vocabulary (purse, duffle, boot, lorry) in an obvious small-scale con
jokes.explanation: Funny but slightly overlong — the list of British terms is good for one beat of comedy but runs a word or two long. Duncan's opportunistic grift works as character comedy but isn't quite as sharp as his earlier lines.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Miss Edison, I find myself in a rather precarious financial position. Might I entreat you for a modest pecuniary accommodation? Perhaps you could see fit to provide me with a small loan, or as we say in the Commonwealth, a spot of readies to tide me over until my next disbursement of remuneration?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Professor Duncan, I have no idea what you just said.

jokes.text: Pierce reveals his 'Ear-Noculars' — a spy earpiece — explaining with pride that 'All hearing is sonic' is answered with 'What's that?'
jokes.setup: Pierce proudly explains that his earpiece is 'Ear-Noculars' that 'give you sonic hearing' for 'spies and whatnot'
jokes.punchline: Jeff correctly points out that 'all hearing is sonic' — and Pierce immediately demonstrates poor hearing by responding 'What's that?'
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed mini-joke. The setup (Pierce's delusional gadget pride) → smart correction ('all hearing is sonic') → instant ironic demonstration ('What's that?') is a three-beat structure firing on all cylinders. The punchline proves the point AND reveals Pierce actually needs hearing aids. Great economy, strong character work, earned laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: These are ear-noculars. They're like binoculars, but for your ears.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: With these, I can hear conversations from across the room. It's like having spy powers.

jokes.text: 'I asked politely, and then panda took his pants off.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is apparently explaining something that happened with a panda, in what seems like a non-sequitur to the ongoing conversation
jokes.punchline: The story concludes with 'panda took his pants off' — the pants-dropping is the punchline to a story we never heard the beginning of
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce absurdism — the joke is that this story began off-screen, was apparently prompted by a conversation about asexuality, and the punchline ('panda took his pants off') answers nothing while raising more questions. The in medias res delivery is the technique, and it's deployed brilliantly for Pierce's character.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not how hearing works, Pierce. Sonic refers to the speed of sound, not the ability to hear it. You're just being annoying.

jokes.text: Troy asks if the experiment 'does stuff to your butt' and when told no, asks if you 'get paid more if they do stuff to your butt'
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to recruit subjects for the psych experiment and mentions they get paid
jokes.punchline: Troy's negotiating position is entirely based on the butt-stuff premium — and when that's not on the table, he still agrees to participate
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy — his escalating butt-stuff inquiry is absurdist but totally in character. The structure is excellent: concern → premium inquiry → shrug-based acceptance. Very Troy-specific. The 'that's fine, I'll do it' despite no premium being offered is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, is this gonna hurt? Because I have a very low pain threshold. I cried during that insurance commercial.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's just a psychology experiment, Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but what if you mess with my brain and I forget how to eat?

jokes.text: Abed: 'They're showing all four Indiana Joneses at the Vista. I'm really looking forward to the first three. I bought a whip.'
jokes.setup: Annie asks Abed to participate in the experiment tomorrow instead of his other plans
jokes.punchline: Abed's response reveals he's already committed to seeing Indiana Jones films — and his deadpan enumeration ('the first three') is both a pop-culture joke and character-defining. 'I bought a whip' is the perfect non-sequitur topper.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Looking forward to the first three' is an economical, perfectly structured burn on Indiana Jones 4 — the implication that the fourth doesn't exist to him is funnier than any direct criticism. 'I bought a whip' is a masterclass in comedy economy: three words that characterize Abed's total commitment to media experiences, delivered with no affect. This line is quotable, character-specific, and structurally perfect. Earns an 8+ comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I can't do the experiment. I bought a whip.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I know what you're thinking: 'Abed, why would you buy a whip?' Well, I saw Kingdom of the Crystal Skull, and I realized that Indiana Jones movies don't need to be good to make me want to be Indiana Jones.

jokes.text: Abed to Annie: 'I figured we were more like Chandler and Phoebe. They never really had stories together.' Then: 'Sure, I'll do it, Chandler.'
jokes.setup: Annie appeals to their friendship to get Abed to come to the experiment
jokes.punchline: Abed processes the relationship in terms of TV character dynamics — identifying them as a low-story pair like Chandler/Phoebe — then immediately accepts and assigns Annie the Chandler role
jokes.explanation: Peak Abed joke — he genuinely models human relationships through TV frameworks, which is both funny and character-illuminating. The Friends reference is used critically, not as fan-service. Calling Annie 'Chandler' (the less glamorous of the two) is a subtle insult wrapped in sincerity. The structure (analysis → reversal → acceptance → role assignment) is impeccable. Very high character integration: only Abed could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You guys are really good friends.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're like Friends. I'm Chandler, Troy's Monica, Shirley's Phoebe, Jeff's Ross, and Britta's Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Why am I Rachel?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because you're the least crucial to the group.

jokes.text: Jeff says about Vaughn: 'Hope he doesn't try to handsome her to death.'
jokes.setup: Jeff watches Vaughn flirting with Britta and decides to intervene
jokes.punchline: 'Handsome her to death' — Jeff acknowledges Vaughn's attractiveness while using it as a dismissive insult, coining a new verb that reveals his jealousy
jokes.explanation: Very economical coinage — 'handsome her to death' as a verb phrase is inventive and characterizes Jeff's particular brand of competitive jealousy: he has to admit Vaughn is attractive while still dismissing him. Economy score is very high — four words carry a full character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He's handsoming her.

jokes.text: Duncan tells Annie to go tell subjects the experiment starts in 5 minutes — then whispers 'It's never actually going to start. Ho ho.'
jokes.setup: Annie is sent to give the waiting subjects a progress update
jokes.punchline: Duncan's aside 'Ho ho' at the end of his cruel deception is a perfectly villainous button — gleeful and slightly unhinged
jokes.explanation: The 'Ho ho' is what elevates this above a standard plot beat — it's both a villain laugh and weirdly avuncular, which is an odd combination that works for Duncan specifically. The conspiratorial aside structure is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Can I just get a coffee?

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Oh man, I can't do that. Coffee's a drug, dude. I'm three years sober from caffeine.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's just coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Just coffee? That's what they all say. One cup leads to two cups, then you're mainlining espresso shots in gas station bathrooms.

jokes.text: Chang's immediate eruption: 'No, no, no! It's unacceptable! When you say something starts at 9:00, it starts at NUEVE!'
jokes.setup: Annie tells the waiting subjects there's a five-minute delay
jokes.punchline: Chang immediately loses his mind, screaming that 9:00 means 'nueve' — a Spanish teacher using Spanish to have a breakdown about punctuality
jokes.explanation: 'It starts at NUEVE' is a gem — using his Spanish-teacher identity to escalate a tantrum about punctuality is exquisitely character-integrated. Chang's hair-trigger volatility is established perfectly in one moment. The word 'nueve' doing the work of a punchline is economy at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: You know, Jeff, I really appreciate you taking the time to share this green tea with me, buddy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, it's... nice.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: I can tell we're really bonding here, chief. This is special, pal.

jokes.text: Chang immediately erupts when told the experiment is running 'a bit behind' — screaming 'When you say something starts at 9:00, it starts at NUEVE!'
jokes.setup: Annie tells the waiting subjects it'll be another five minutes
jokes.punchline: Chang's instant, disproportionate breakdown includes switching to Spanish for '9' in a moment of maximum absurdity, as if Spanish proves his point more forcefully
jokes.explanation: The pivot to 'nueve' is inspired — Chang is a Spanish teacher, so using Spanish in his tantrum is both character-integrated and perfectly absurd. It simultaneously reveals he's always 'performing' his Spanish teacherness even in crisis. Very quotable. 'It starts at nueve!' is the kind of line that gets repeated.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Annie, go tell them we'll start in five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, Professor Duncan.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: There are no subjects. There is no study. I just wanted to see if she'd do whatever I asked.

jokes.text: Duncan observes Chang's tantrum through the one-way glass: 'Houston, we have an idiot.'
jokes.setup: Chang erupts in an immediate, disproportionate tantrum at the five-minute delay
jokes.punchline: Duncan's NASA quote riff — replacing 'problem' with 'idiot' — is a dry, dismissive assessment
jokes.explanation: A reliable template joke (famous quote with one word swapped) but executed with good timing and appropriate dryness. 'Houston, we have a problem' riffs are not novel, but 'idiot' as the replacement word is satisfying. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're running behind.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Running behind?! Do you know what time it is?! This is unacceptable! We were supposed to be there an hour ago! An hour! That's like... nine in Spanish!

jokes.text: During Shirley and Jeff's walk, Jeff starts to ask a question and Shirley cuts in with 'So you've got a kid, right?' — Jeff says 'What's that? Nothing.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley are attempting the long walk across campus Jeff dreaded
jokes.punchline: The conversation is so stilted they talk over each other, and Jeff immediately retreats with 'Nothing' when caught — proving his fears about the walk were warranted
jokes.explanation: A quiet, structural callback to Jeff's sprint/marathon metaphor. The awkwardness pays off the setup but isn't a particularly strong joke on its own — it's more of a beat confirming what we already knew. Functional cringe rather than a sharp joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Houston, we have a problem!

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: That's not even close to what's happening right now.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'I know a lot of grown men with radar dishes coming out of their ear.' Jeff: '[laughs] He's like Inspector Gadget.' Shirley: 'Yeah, go go gadget incontinence.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley bond over Pierce's ear devices — Jeff makes the Inspector Gadget comparison
jokes.punchline: Shirley escalates it perfectly: 'Go go gadget incontinence' — aging Pierce's gadget persona with an age-appropriate malfunction
jokes.explanation: A great escalation joke. Jeff provides the reference ('Inspector Gadget') and Shirley immediately builds on it with 'go go gadget incontinence' — which is both the right format (gadget + function) and a sharp, specific-to-Pierce dig about age. The collaborative structure between two characters makes it feel organic. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'd love to walk with you, Jeff. But I have to warn you — I walk really slow because my legs are so short.

jokes.text: 'He's like Inspector Gadget.' / 'Yeah, go, go, gadget incontinence.'
jokes.setup: Shirley makes a Inspector Gadget comparison for Pierce's ear device
jokes.punchline: Jeff riffs on the Inspector Gadget catchphrase — 'Go go gadget incontinence' — adding an age-appropriate ailment as the gadget
jokes.explanation: Clean riff — takes the Inspector Gadget setup and deploys 'incontinence' as the gadget, which is both age-appropriate for Pierce and an unexpected word to follow the catchphrase structure. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, Pierce is totally normal. He's just a regular guy who happens to think that yogurt is a government conspiracy and that his skin condition is caused by witches.

jokes.text: Jeff says Vaughn's hair is 'perpetually moist'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley are gossiping about Vaughn and his flirtatious behavior with Britta
jokes.punchline: 'Perpetually moist' — a strangely specific and viscerally unpleasant descriptor that works as an insult precisely because of the word 'moist'
jokes.explanation: 'Perpetually moist' is two words doing huge work — 'moist' is universally uncomfortable, and 'perpetually' implies it never improves. The choice of adjective is carefully considered comedy writing. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Pierce, you're like Inspector Gadget, except all your gadgets are just different ways your body is falling apart.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Go go gadget hip replacement!

jokes.text: Duncan's color commentary on the waiting subjects: 'We've got a shouter... that one's a stomper... there's a generic whack job, bouncing up and down like a six-foot child... visible shakes... it's like Benny Hill looks.'
jokes.setup: Three hours into the wait, Duncan reviews the subjects' breaking points with Annie and Troy
jokes.punchline: Duncan's detached, sports-commentary framing of human suffering — categorizing people's breakdowns as 'types' — is both darkly funny and revealing of his professional detachment
jokes.explanation: The catalog of breakdown types is funny as a running list, and 'six-foot child' is a sharp specific image. The Benny Hill reference works because Duncan controls the speed of the collapse like a director. Good sustained bit but no single line stands out as exceptional.

jokes.text: Duncan does Benny Hill-style commentary as he speeds up the camera footage: 'Whoo, ooh, ooh, get him. Come back again. Whoo, ooh, ooh, get him. All right? There's a bit of fun. It lightens the mood.'
jokes.setup: Duncan is reviewing footage of subjects chasing each other
jokes.punchline: He narrates the sped-up footage with Benny Hill sound effects and then sincerely says 'There's a bit of fun. It lightens the mood.' — as if he's doing the subjects a favor
jokes.explanation: The Benny Hill reference is well-deployed and appropriately British for Duncan. 'It lightens the mood' as a sincere self-justification for sadism is a good button. Entertaining but not among the episode's sharpest.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: This is fascinating. Look at the way Subject 7 is experiencing acute psychological distress. The way he's flailing about, the desperation in his voice... it's like watching a perfectly timed pratfall.

jokes.text: Troy's breakdown after 26+ hours: 'The Soul Train Awards were tonight. You promised butt stuff!' [crying]
jokes.setup: Troy has been waiting in the room for 26+ hours, and Duncan announces there are only 'two subjects left'
jokes.punchline: Troy's breakdown prioritizes Soul Train Awards and the promised-but-nonexistent butt stuff — a callback to his recruitment question — in a list of genuine grievances
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback payoff. The butt stuff comes back as a legitimately felt betrayal rather than just a throwaway gag, which is excellent structural writing. Soul Train Awards as a competing priority is perfectly Troy. The crying makes it cringe-funny. 'You promised butt stuff!' is an instantly quotable line. High impact, strong character integration, earned laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I've been waiting here for SEVEN HOURS. Seven hours! Do you know what I could've been doing? Studying! Sleeping! Literally anything but standing here like a idiot!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And THEN—THEN!—someone ate my yogurt. MY yogurt. The one I labeled. With my name on it. In permanent marker!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: But that's not even the worst part. The WORST part is that I'm pretty sure it was the MANGO yogurt. Who steals mango? MANGO?! That's the worst flavor!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And now my shirt has a wrinkle in it. A WRINKLE. One wrinkle, and it's permanent. I'm going to have to throw out this entire shirt. This is a $40 shirt!

jokes.text: Duncan: 'And he's out. We got him. Strike three. You're gone.' — gleefully celebrating Troy's breakdown as a sporting victory
jokes.setup: Troy breaks down crying
jokes.punchline: Duncan celebrates using baseball elimination language as if this is a sports broadcast, completely disconnected from the human suffering he's caused
jokes.explanation: Decent but slightly repetitive of the earlier sports commentary mode. The baseball metaphor is functional, but the comedy comes more from context than from the line itself. Duncan's sociopathic detachment is well-established by this point.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Why aren't you two together? You're both so attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, Shirley, it's a little more complicated than that.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: No it's not. You're white, she's cute. Done.

jokes.text: Duncan: 'The longer they wait, the harder they break. Buckle up, students.' [both laughing]
jokes.setup: Only two subjects remain after the mass exodus
jokes.punchline: 'Buckle up, students' — Duncan adopts the teacher role to coach his students in enjoying the sadistic spectacle, the irony being he's the worst person in the room
jokes.explanation: The 'students' address inverts the teacher/student dynamic pleasantly but doesn't quite land as a strong individual joke. More of a tone-setter for the scene than a punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Vaughn seems cool.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: He is! He's really into yogurt and the environment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh no.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'I don't see why you and Britta aren't together. Two cute white people, going to school together — just seems right.'
jokes.setup: Shirley and Jeff are gossiping about Vaughn and Britta
jokes.punchline: Shirley's reasoning for why Jeff and Britta should be together — 'two cute white people' — is delivered as self-evident logic, exposing her own assumptions about racial pairing while being completely sincere
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Shirley says the quiet part loud — the racial pairings logic that people think but don't say — delivered with total innocence. It's sharp social observation disguised as matchmaking advice. Character-specific: Shirley's well-meaning but oblivious quality is perfectly deployed.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Shirley, we're not pandas in a zoo.'
jokes.setup: Shirley says two cute white people going to school together 'just seems right'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pandas-in-a-zoo metaphor reframes the breeding-pair logic Shirley is applying — matching white people like conservation efforts
jokes.explanation: A genuinely exceptional line. Six words that perfectly capture what Shirley was implying (endangered-species pairing) while recontextualizing it as absurd. 'Pandas in a zoo' is an inspired image — specific, funny, and a perfect rebuke. Economy is near-perfect. This is the kind of line that writers are proud of. Earns its 8+ comparison.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going to friend you so hard, Vaughn. I'm going to friend you with the power of a thousand suns. I'm going to friend you until you don't even know what friending means anymore.

jokes.text: Jeff's reaction shot: 'That is not what I want to see.' — looking at Vaughn and Britta in the quad
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley are gossiping about Vaughn and Britta while watching them from across campus
jokes.punchline: Jeff's pained, involuntary response to seeing Vaughn and Britta together confirms the jealousy he's been denying — 'that is not what I want to see' is both literal and emotionally revealing
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat than a joke, but the involuntary admission functions as comedy. Jeff's affectless delivery of sincere emotion is consistent character work. Not a strong standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: His nipples are smaller than my children's hamsters.

jokes.text: 'There goes the shirt.' — Vaughn removes his shirt in the quad
jokes.setup: Jeff previously complained Vaughn 'plays shirts and skins in a game of checkers'
jokes.punchline: The shirt removal is confirmed — Vaughn really does just take his shirt off, validating Jeff's characterization
jokes.explanation: A visual callback that pays off a good earlier line. The payoff itself is simpler than the setup — 'there goes the shirt' is minimal — but it validates the prediction and lands the visual gag. Functions better as confirmation than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's been 26 hours.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Just five more minutes.

jokes.text: Jeff claims to Britta 'Vaughn seems cool' — then grimaces and says 'That was tacky out there. You won't ever see that again.' Then Vaughn says 'No worries, brah.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to prove he's not a jerk by being gracious about Vaughn in front of Britta
jokes.punchline: The moment Britta leaves, Jeff immediately breaks character and apologizes to himself for saying Vaughn is cool. Vaughn's oblivious 'No worries, brah' is a perfect button.
jokes.explanation: Jeff's immediate self-flagellation for the compliment is good character work — he can't sustain the act even for a moment once Britta is gone. 'That was tacky out there' as self-criticism is a funny self-aware confession. Vaughn's breezy non-response is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: You know what? You're like Mark David Chapman.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What? Why would you say that?

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Because you just shot my experiment dead.

jokes.text: Shirley mentions Senor Chang's socks: 'Tiny bullfighters.' Jeff and Shirley laugh together.
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley continue their gossip session, now bonding over Chang
jokes.punchline: 'Tiny bullfighters' — the specificity of the sock pattern is funnier than a generic sock joke would be. It's an absurd detail that tells you everything about Chang's personality.
jokes.explanation: Two words doing a lot of work. 'Tiny bullfighters' is specific enough to be clearly visualizable and absurd enough to be funny on its own. The image of Chang wearing novelty bullfighter socks fits his character. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Abed, you've contaminated my entire experiment! Do you understand what you've done?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I was just trying to help.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Help? You're a statistical anomaly. A complete outlier. In fact, I'm going to have to recalibrate my entire methodology because of you. You fall so far outside the normal distribution, you're essentially a data point that invalidates the entire dataset.

jokes.text: Shirley tops Jeff's socks observation: 'Did you see that Hacky Sack wears an anklet?'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley's gossip session escalates; Jeff mentions Chang's socks
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately one-ups with the anklet detail — the fact that she's catalogued this about Vaughn suggests she's been noticing him more than she admits
jokes.explanation: Good pot-stirrer characterization for Shirley. 'An anklet' as a detail about Vaughn is well-chosen — it's both crunchy-hippie-accurate and slightly emasculating in Shirley's framing.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: You're a... you're a... FANNY!

jokes.text: Jeff says he wants to 'friend the hell out of that green-tea-drinking drum circler'
jokes.setup: Jeff claims he wants to prove he's not a jerk by genuinely befriending Vaughn
jokes.punchline: 'Friend the hell out of' — weaponizing friendship as an aggressive act, plus the stacking of Vaughn's hippie descriptors ('green-tea-drinking drum circler') as a dismissive compound noun
jokes.explanation: Jeff turning friendship into an aggressive project is very Jeff. The hyphenated insult-descriptor for Vaughn is good — it compounds multiple earlier jokes (green tea, drumming, hippie) into a single dismissive phrase. The verb 'friend the hell out of' is inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Professor Duncan
dialogue.line: Blblblblbl

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Okay, but tell me you've noticed how small his nipples are.' Then: 'It's not gossip when it's fact. My kids have got hamsters with bigger nips.'
jokes.setup: Jeff refuses to engage with more gossip about Vaughn to prove he's a good friend to Britta
jokes.punchline: Shirley's defense of nipple-size observation as empirical fact — not gossip — is an absurd epistemological argument, escalated by the hamster comparison
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. 'It's not gossip when it's fact' as a philosophical defense is brilliantly self-justifying, and 'my kids have got hamsters with bigger nips' is a spectacular escalation — specific, visual, deeply Shirley, and completely unexpected. The hamster comparison is the kind of line that gets rewound. Very high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So how's the community service going?

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Oh man, it's been a really profound experience. I've been teaching elderly people frisbee, and it's like, they've lived all these years without knowing the beauty of the disc, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's frisbee, Vaughn.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Exactly. And now they know.

jokes.text: Abed is revealed to still be sitting motionless in the waiting room 26+ hours later — 'Is it on pause? No, that's just him.'
jokes.setup: Duncan shows the monitor of the remaining subjects — there are only two left
jokes.punchline: Abed appears completely still, like a frozen video — and the reveal is that he's not frozen, he's just sitting perfectly motionless
jokes.explanation: A great Abed joke that works on multiple levels: it's funny visually (he looks like a paused video), it's character-defining (Abed is so internally preoccupied he can sit completely still for 26 hours without distress), and 'that's just him' is a perfect deadpan explanation. The setup (is it on pause?) is a great misdirection before the character-based punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What makes frisbee ultimate?

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Well, that's like asking what makes Ultimate Frisbee ultimate. It's the ultimate of frisbee.

jokes.text: Abed, sitting alone in the waiting room after 26 hours — 'Is it on pause?' / 'No, that's just him.'
jokes.setup: Abed is completely still in the waiting room after 26 hours; Duncan and Annie observe him on the monitor
jokes.punchline: Duncan asks if the feed is 'on pause' — implying Abed is so motionless he looks like a frozen screen — and Annie confirms it's just Abed
jokes.explanation: Beautiful Abed joke — his stillness being mistaken for a frozen video feed is perfectly in character (Abed processes the world differently and doesn't waste energy on waiting-room fidgeting). The two-line exchange is very economical. 'No, that's just him' is a great punchline. High craft.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: It's called 'the bee' because it flies, man. Ultimate frisbee isn't just a sport—it's a way of life. It's about freedom, about soaring above the constraints of society.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: My grandfather plays shuffleboard, and you know what? That's profound too. We're all just trying to find meaning in the flight of our projectiles.

jokes.text: Duncan to Annie: 'Go kill John Lennon again, you loser.'
jokes.setup: Annie interrupts the experiment to say she has classes and needs to leave
jokes.punchline: Duncan's exit insult — equating her departure with Mark David Chapman's act — is so disproportionately dark it circles back to funny
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly dark line for a network sitcom. The disproportionality is what makes it funny — Annie asking to leave classes is compared to killing John Lennon. It says more about Duncan's mental state than Annie's betrayal. The 'again' implies she's a repeat offender.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: ¿Habla usted español? Mi amigo, yo tengo... uh... los pantalones con queso.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Dude, I think you just told me you have pants with cheese.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Sí, sí, very good! Your Spanish is... wait, no.

jokes.text: Duncan: 'He has warped the Duncan Principle! Damn you, you outlying piece of datum!' [bangs head, screams]
jokes.setup: Abed still hasn't broken after 26+ hours, ruining Duncan's experiment
jokes.punchline: Duncan's academic language ('outlying piece of datum') applied to a full emotional breakdown is a perfect irony — the psychologist studying ego loss completely loses his own ego
jokes.explanation: The Duncan Principle claims the ego breaks under lost control — and Abed causes Duncan to perfectly illustrate his own principle by breaking down. 'Outlying piece of datum' as an insult is inspired: the clinical vocabulary in a moment of pure emotional collapse is a classic incongruity joke. Great structural irony. The 'ow!' after banging his head is a nice physical button.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, um... 'Wizard blue, wizard true, wizard me, wizard you.' This doesn't even rhyme!

jokes.text: Duncan to Annie: 'Not Rain Man! I should never have let you into this lab, Miss Annie Fanny Panties in a Bunch!'
jokes.setup: Duncan blames Annie for bringing Abed as a subject
jokes.punchline: 'Miss Annie Fanny Panties in a Bunch' — a full-breakdown nickname that rhymes and unravels simultaneously, the insult collapsing under its own weight
jokes.explanation: The nickname is funny primarily because of its escalation into incoherence — it starts as an insult and devolves into a rhyme scheme that undercuts any authority Duncan had. The Rain Man comparison for Abed is also a solid character note. Duncan's breakdown mirroring the subjects' breakdowns is the structural payoff of the whole experiment plot.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so Vaughn wrote this poem, and it's... it's really bad. Like, objectively terrible. But here's the thing - there are actual tear stains on the paper. So either Vaughn cried while writing this, or he cried while reading it, which somehow makes it worse.

jokes.text: Annie retorts: 'Did you think of that the last time you skipped a trip to the dentist?' — Duncan responds by blowing a raspberry
jokes.setup: Duncan insults Annie with a playground-level nickname; Annie counter-attacks
jokes.punchline: Duncan's response to Annie's dentist crack is a literal raspberry — two adults completely abandoning adult behavior simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Annie giving as good as she gets is a good character moment, and Duncan's raspberry is a perfect infantile response from someone who's supposedly a psychology authority. The escalation of their mutual breakdown is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I couldn't leave. You guys are my friends.

jokes.text: Duncan's full meltdown: 'It's not fair! It's not fair! Stop writing! Put your pen— Give me that! Get out! Get out, you dorks! Get out! YOU HAVE DESTROYED THE DUNCAN PRINCIPLE!'
jokes.setup: Duncan has been unraveling throughout the scene — the final escalation point
jokes.punchline: Duncan completely fulfills the Duncan Principle — the psychologist studying ego loss loses his own ego, becoming the experiment's most perfect subject
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the entire experiment subplot — the psychologist who designed a test of ego resilience perfectly illustrates his own principle by catastrophically failing it. 'You have destroyed the Duncan Principle!' is the topper, with the irony that he's simultaneously proving it. This is earned comedy through story structure — the kind of payoff that makes a room erupt on rewatch because you see it coming and it still delivers. Very high earned vs. cheap score.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know you've all been talking about me behind my back. I have proof.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I planted a listening device in the study room. It's disguised as a decorative pen. Cost me $400.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Pierce, that's insane. You can't just spy on us.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Oh, but I can. And I did. For three weeks.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What did you hear?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Everything. And frankly, I'm hurt. You all said my stories are boring.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, joke's on you. That pen also records in HD. I'm selling the footage to a reality TV producer.

jokes.text: Abed's final exit from the experiment room: 'Cool. See ya.'
jokes.setup: Duncan has just had a complete breakdown and thrown everyone out of the lab
jokes.punchline: After 26+ hours of motionless waiting and precipitating a psychologist's breakdown, Abed's only response is 'Cool. See ya.' — absolutely unbothered
jokes.explanation: Three words that are perfectly Abed. The joke is entirely in the juxtaposition: catastrophic experiment meltdown → 'Cool. See ya.' delivered with zero affect. Only Abed, who has been entirely present through 26 hours without distress, could exit this way. Maximum economy — literally nothing could be added without weakening it. One of the episode's finest character moments.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: He claims to have six-pack abs and describes his hair as moist.

jokes.text: Vaughn asks Jeff what makes frisbee 'ultimate' and says 'If I had a nickel for every time I wished somebody asked me that'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks Vaughn an innocuous question to 'friend the hell out of him'
jokes.punchline: Vaughn's enthusiasm about being asked the ultimate frisbee question reveals he thinks about it constantly — the gap between his passion and others' indifference is the joke
jokes.explanation: Decent character joke that establishes Vaughn's earnest cluelessness. The 'nickel for every time' inversion (he wishes people asked, implying they never do) is good, but it's a small beat in a scene designed to show Jeff suffering through niceness.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Is he the guy with the weird thing?

jokes.text: Britta and Jeff's conversation about Vaughn saying things 'after...' with Shirley supplying increasingly euphemistic guesses: 'School? Dinner mints? Not having sex?'
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to tell Jeff that Vaughn says things 'after...' — unable to say 'sex' in front of Shirley
jokes.punchline: Shirley's escalating guesses land on 'not having sex?' as her final try — the euphemism more awkward than the word itself
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed escalating guessing game. The list structure (school → dinner mints → not having sex) creates a nice rhythm where 'not having sex' is funnier than 'sex' would have been because it's a double negative that makes no sense as a euphemism. Character-specific: Shirley's discomfort with adult topics makes her guesses simultaneously too prudish and too close.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Vaughn has this thing where he says 'hey' at the beginning and end of every sentence. 'Hey, how are you? Hey.' It's like verbal bookends.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Herpes?' when Britta says Vaughn 'gave her something'
jokes.setup: Britta says 'He gave me something' — a phrase open to multiple interpretations
jokes.punchline: Shirley immediately guesses 'Herpes?' — the dark interpretation delivered in Shirley's chipper register
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the dark interpretation of an innocent phrase. The joke is in the character: Shirley's sunny delivery of 'Herpes?' makes it funnier than it would be from a cynical character. One word, good economy, slightly predictable structure but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Hey! Hey! Hey! What's up, Jeff? How are you doing? How are you feeling? How are you?

jokes.text: Shirley receives Vaughn's poem by text and reads it aloud: 'Did you ever notice where the ocean meets the sky, did ya? / It's the same wizard blue that I see in your eye, Brit-Ta.'
jokes.setup: Shirley pretends to get a text and reads it, saying she will answer Britta's question about the poem
jokes.punchline: The poem is catastrophically bad — 'wizard blue,' the forced meter of 'Brit-Ta,' and the earnestness of the whole thing make it funnier than any deliberate parody
jokes.explanation: The poem is a great piece of comedy writing — it has to be authentically bad poetry while also being funny. 'Wizard blue' is an inspired choice of terrible adjective (not quite right for the register, slightly fantasy-novel). 'Brit-Ta' as a forced two-syllable rhyme is the topper. Britta's immediate 'Oh no no, wizard blue?!' is the right audience surrogate reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: What? Why is everyone laughing? Did I say something funny? I was just trying to be helpful. You guys are being really mean right now. This is like that time in third grade when everyone made fun of my lunch box because it had my name on it in puffy paint. I worked really hard on that puffy paint.

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Oh, he said "rad"? I thought he said "bad." Oh, that makes it worse.'
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals the word Vaughn cried over is 'rad'
jokes.punchline: Shirley's misreading ('bad' instead of 'rad') is immediately corrected — but her response ('that makes it worse') reframes 'rad' as more damning than 'bad' would have been
jokes.explanation: A quick, elegant beat — the reversal of 'that makes it worse' after the correction is the kind of reaction that works because it's exactly right. 'Bad' would be sad; 'rad' implies Vaughn was aiming for enthusiasm and crying about it. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Vaughn
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Are you guys making fun of me right now? Because that's not cool, man. That's not cool at all. You know what? This hurts. This really hurts. And I'm gonna describe it using my own slang because that's how I express myself: Dude, you just gave me a major bummer-downer.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm surprised he can read.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley's roast of Vaughn continues
jokes.punchline: Jeff's escalation to questioning Vaughn's basic literacy is a satisfying progression of contempt delivered with perfect deadpan
jokes.explanation: A reliable escalation beat — not especially original but lands because of the deadpan and the rhythm of the gossip session. 'I'm surprised he can read' as a logical endpoint of the contempt escalation makes contextual sense even if it's not a particularly inventive line.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I have a problem. I'm addicted to gossip. I can't help myself. I see someone and I just have to tell everyone their business.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My therapist says it's a control issue, but what does she know? She's just sitting there listening to me all day.

jokes.text: Annie: '"Gotcha"? That's all you have to say? You sat in a room for 26 straight hours. Didn't that bother you?' Troy: 'Yeah, I was livid.' Annie: 'Then why didn't you leave?' Troy: 'Because you asked me to stay and you said we were friends.'
jokes.setup: Annie is shocked Troy isn't upset about the experiment deception
jokes.punchline: Troy's revelation that he WAS livid but stayed anyway because Annie said they were friends — his loyalty overriding his outrage — recontextualizes his earlier '26 hours' breakdown as stoic suffering for a friend
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly warm and structurally excellent joke. The reveal (he WAS livid, but stayed for friendship) completely reframes the experiment — Troy is not oblivious, he's loyal. 'You said we were friends' as the total explanation is both funny and genuinely touching. This joke does double duty: lands as comedy and deepens Troy's character. High earned score.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I know what people say about me. They think I'm all sweetness and light, like a cute little bumblebee. But let me tell you something—bumblebees sting. And I will sting you.

jokes.text: Annie asks 'Is this still part of the experiment?' after Troy's sincere answer
jokes.setup: Troy gives an unexpectedly sincere and emotionally honest answer about friendship
jokes.punchline: Annie's reflexive suspicion that sincerity might itself be a manipulation is a good meta-beat about the experiment's after-effects
jokes.explanation: A quick, structural joke that works as a button to the Troy/Annie scene. The paranoia about sincerity being experimental manipulation is a funny consequence of running psychological experiments on your friends.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: What are we gonna talk about if we don't have gossip?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh my God... we have nothing in common.

jokes.text: Duncan describes Abed: 'He's more like a puppy with a fish mouth' and both he and Annie attempt fish-mouth impressions
jokes.setup: Duncan and Annie discuss why Abed didn't break in the experiment
jokes.punchline: 'Puppy with a fish mouth' as an Abed description is specific and strange — and both characters then apparently perform the impression simultaneously
jokes.explanation: 'Puppy with a fish mouth' is a good absurdist image — puppies are cute and loyal, fish mouths are weird and unreadable, and their combination captures Abed's particular blend of eager and alien. The shared impression is a good visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Okay, you know what? I'm done gossiping. From this moment on, I'm a new woman. No more talking about other people's business.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh my God, did you know that Dean Pelton has been ordering women's shoes to his office? Size 10!

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I heard you with my own ear... noculars.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just confronted the group for making fun of him
jokes.punchline: Pierce's triumphant use of the Ear-Noculars to catch them in the act is immediately undercut by his pause before '...noculars' — he almost forgot the word he made up
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback joke. 'Ear... noculars' with the pause suggests Pierce briefly forgot his own coinage — which is funnier than if he'd said it confidently. It simultaneously pays off the Ear-Noculars setup, reveals they actually worked, and self-deprecates through the hesitation. Very quotable. The triple function makes it one of the episode's structural highlights.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I only bought the first three Indiana Jones movies.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Why not the fourth one?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It doesn't exist.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It doesn't exist.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Uh-huh. Calling me "Hacky Sack" and ripping on my six-pack abs and my moist hair.'
jokes.setup: Pierce confronts the group for mocking him, listing what he heard
jokes.punchline: Pierce conflates 'Hacky Sack' (his nickname for Vaughn) with himself — plus 'moist hair' was about Vaughn, not Pierce — revealing he only partially understood what he overheard
jokes.explanation: Pierce's misunderstanding — attributing Vaughn-mockery to himself — is both funny and character-revealing: he's so self-focused he assumes everything negative is about him. 'Six-pack abs' as a point of pride is a good absurdist detail for a man who clearly has none.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, let's be clear about what this is. We're friends. But I need to establish some parameters here. Friendship isn't some nebulous emotional contract—it's a technical specification. You've got your core friend functions, your optional friend modules, and your friendship-breaking bugs that void the whole agreement.

jokes.text: Pierce says 'Oh, good' when told the mockery was about Vaughn — then immediately adds 'Maybe he has a tiny penis.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is relieved to learn the mockery wasn't about him
jokes.punchline: Pierce pivots instantly from aggrieved victim to enthusiastic gossip participant with his first contribution: genital speculation
jokes.explanation: The speed of Pierce's reversal — from outraged victim to enthusiastic gossip — and the specific nature of his first contribution (penis size) is very Pierce. It says everything about his character: grievances are entirely transactional, and he has no filter. Good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, but what if we were just friends who occasionally hang out and text each other memes?

jokes.text: Pierce's impression of Vaughn: 'Everything's all "no worries, no worries" and he always says hello three times in a row: "Hello, good evening, how are you?"'
jokes.setup: Pierce joins the gossip session and offers his own Vaughn observations
jokes.punchline: Pierce's characterization of Vaughn's triple-greeting as a tick is oddly specific and accurate — 'Hello, good evening, how are you?' as three separate hellos is a good observation
jokes.explanation: Pierce's observation about Vaughn's triple greeting is accurate and mildly funny, but the joke is more structural (setting up the Vaughn-enters-and-does-exactly-that payoff) than comedic on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Look, the human ear wasn't meant to see that far. We're not evolved for it. God gave us ears for a reason — to hear things close by, like our loved ones telling us we're great.

jokes.text: Pierce shows the group Vaughn's poem on his phone — 'Why is the dinosaur rocking a picture of my poem?' — Vaughn has arrived and seen the whole thing
jokes.setup: Pierce is about to show the poem to the group; Vaughn walks in
jokes.punchline: Vaughn's question about the 'dinosaur' (presumably Pierce's phone case) holding his poem is an absurdist detail that breaks the tension of the reveal — 'dinosaur' as a phone case being the strangest detail to focus on in a humiliating moment
jokes.explanation: The 'dinosaur' detail is an inspired touch — in the middle of his public humiliation, Vaughn focuses on the most irrelevant possible detail (Pierce's phone case). This both characterizes Vaughn's slightly off-center attention and gives Pierce's tech eccentricity another beat.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, as you get older, your hearing goes. First the high frequencies disappear, then the lows. Eventually, all you can hear is the mid-range where human voices live. It's like God's way of making sure that no matter how deaf you become, you can still hear the people you love.

jokes.text: Vaughn: 'This is the least tight thing that's ever happened to me.'
jokes.setup: Vaughn realizes the whole group has been mocking him and his poem
jokes.punchline: Vaughn processes maximum public humiliation through his own slang vocabulary — 'least tight' as a measure of awfulness is a good character-specific deflation
jokes.explanation: A great callback to Vaughn's vocabulary — 'tight' has been established as his superlative, so 'least tight' as the worst thing is perfectly in character. The understatement of using slang to process profound public humiliation is excellent economy. This is a satisfying payoff to Vaughn's characterization throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Mon, Desperate Housewives is de best show on television, mon!

jokes.text: Duncan's reaction observation: 'He's crying. Now he's barking.'
jokes.setup: Vaughn is having an emotional breakdown after seeing the group mock him
jokes.punchline: 'Now he's barking' — Duncan's clinical, dispassionate blow-by-blow of Vaughn's breakdown, including the apparently unprecedented detail of barking
jokes.explanation: 'Now he's barking' — four words that do enormous work because we have to infer from the phrasing that Vaughn is making some kind of unhinged vocalization. The clinical voice (he's crying / now he's barking) is Duncan's perfect register. Very economic.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Doogie Howser, M.D., here. I'm a young prodigy, but I'm also tired all the time. Hi, I'm Ryan Seacrest, and I'm exhausted. I've been doing this since I was 16 years old. My back hurts, my knees are shot. I'm only 26!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Britta is never gonna forgive me. I can't believe I showed you that poem. Oh my god, my life is Degrassi High.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is mortified by the Vaughn situation spiraling
jokes.punchline: 'My life is Degrassi High' — Jeff comparing his current social drama to a teen soap opera is both self-aware and character-specific for someone who considers himself above such things
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware moment for Jeff — his horror at social drama he created is best expressed through a teen-drama reference. 'Degrassi High' is a specific and apt choice. Character-consistent with Jeff's self-image as someone above community college social politics.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Can you guys keep it down? Some of us are trying to enjoy our narcissism in peace!

jokes.text: Shirley: 'Oh, Jeff. I have a gossip problem. I stir the pot, Jeff. I'm a pot stirrer. This isn't even the only study group I've had this year. You see those ladies over there? I used to be in their group till they kicked me out. They call me "Tattle-Ina." It's a bumblebee nickname. It's cute but it stings.'
jokes.setup: Shirley and Jeff are both feeling guilty about their gossip session and its consequences
jokes.punchline: Shirley's confession escalates from 'I have a problem' to multiple study groups, to a nickname ('Tattle-Ina'), to her explanation of the nickname as 'a bumblebee nickname — cute but it stings'
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered confession that escalates beautifully. 'Tattle-Ina' is an inspired nickname — it rhymes with 'Tina' and captures the gossip habit in one word. But the real joke is the explanation: 'a bumblebee nickname — it's cute but it stings.' This is Shirley's character in a sentence: she finds something cute and threatening simultaneously and can't tell which aspect to lead with. Very high character integration. Genuinely quotable.

jokes.text: Jeff looks at another table and says 'Hey, look at the size of that woman's earrings. It's like little dogs should be jumping through them.' Shirley immediately responds: 'Mmmmmmmm!'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley just agreed to stop gossiping and snarking on people
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately breaks the pact with an observation about earrings — Shirley's 'Mmmmmm!' reveals she immediately wants to engage even as she's trying to resist
jokes.explanation: Good irony — the gossip pact dissolves instantly. The earring image is funny ('little dogs jumping through them'), and Shirley's involuntary 'Mmmmmm!' suggests her desire to participate can't be suppressed. Character-consistent for both of them.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Come on, what are we gonna talk about? My kids? Your doctor career?' Shirley: 'I was a lawyer.' Shirley: 'See? I'm already bored.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley try to find something to talk about that isn't gossip
jokes.punchline: Jeff knows so little about Shirley he can't name any of her life details accurately — she doesn't have a 'doctor career' — and when corrected, he admits boredom before she can
jokes.explanation: Jeff confusing Shirley's career (and not even having the right profession) is a good character beat — he genuinely doesn't know anything about her beyond her role as gossip partner. 'I was a lawyer' (correcting Shirley's details about Jeff) followed by 'I'm already bored' — wait, the attributions in the transcript flip here, making this slightly more complex, but the comedic point stands: neither knows the other beyond snark. Functional.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'We'll always have "tiny nipples."' [Shirley laughs] 'They were tiny.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley acknowledge their gossip-based friendship cannot be reformed
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames their shared mockery of Vaughn's nipples as a 'Casablanca'-style romantic memory ('We'll always have Paris') — Shirley's confirming 'They were tiny' treats it with the same nostalgic gravity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Applying the Casablanca romantic farewell structure to nipple commentary is an inspired juxtaposition. 'We'll always have tiny nipples' as the shared memory that defines their friendship is absurd and perfect. Shirley's earnest confirmation ('They were tiny') treats it with the gravity of a war-time romance. This is exactly the kind of reference-parodying that Community does best — the form is elevated, the content is lowbrow, the combination is gold. High originality, structure, earned scores.

jokes.text: Shirley whispers: 'Britta told me she had a sex dream about you. You still have a chance.' [squeals]
jokes.setup: Jeff and Shirley are saying their bittersweet gossip-friendship farewell
jokes.punchline: Shirley, in the same breath as her resolve to be better, delivers one final devastating piece of gossip — proving she cannot help herself
jokes.explanation: The perfect button for Shirley's gossip arc — she can't resist. The delivery of a sex dream revelation as a final gift shows Shirley's character is irremediable in the best way. 'You still have a chance' as encouragement to Jeff is a funny callback to his pursuit of Britta that's been dormant in the episode.

jokes.text: Annie apologizes to Abed and gives him the first three Indiana Jones films on DVD. Abed says 'Indiana Jones, cool' — they simultaneously say 'the fourth one blows'
jokes.setup: Annie is apologizing for yelling at Abed and brings a peace offering
jokes.punchline: Annie and Abed's simultaneous 'the fourth one blows' — completing each other's shared aesthetic value judgment — is both a friendship beat and a callback to Abed's earlier 'first three' line
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff — Annie has absorbed Abed's view, and their simultaneous delivery suggests a genuine friendship forming around shared cultural opinions. 'The fourth one blows' as a bonding moment is a nice Community touch: relationships formed through pop culture consensus.

jokes.text: Jeff to Britta: 'I couldn't handle just being one of the girls.' Britta: 'What do you want to be?' Jeff: 'Is there a spot on the friendship spectrum between total stranger and having to hear about the guys you date? And ideally just a notch underneath driving you to the airport and painting your kitchen?'
jokes.setup: Jeff is apologizing to Britta and trying to explain his behavior throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: Jeff's precise taxonomy of friendship obligations — the 'airport run' and 'kitchen painting' as the top of the friendship pyramid he's trying to avoid — is a very specific and funny articulation of commitment anxiety
jokes.explanation: Jeff's friendship-spectrum taxonomy is very Jeff — the analytical mind applied to emotional avoidance. 'Painting your kitchen' and 'driving you to the airport' as the ultimate friendship obligations is culturally specific and funny. The logic is sound (he wants relationship benefits without obligations), which makes it funnier than arbitrary dodging.

jokes.text: Britta: 'How about the friend level where you sometimes have to cat-sit?' Jeff: 'Done.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just laid out his precise friendship demands — below airport runs and kitchen painting
jokes.punchline: Britta offers a lesser obligation (cat-sitting) and Jeff immediately accepts — he has zero attachment issues with cats
jokes.explanation: 'Done.' as a one-word acceptance is perfect economy — it ends the negotiation instantly and reveals Jeff is entirely consistent in his logic. The cat-sit is exactly the right level for him. Good structure.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'And if I'm occasionally naked in your dreams, I won't complain.'
jokes.setup: Jeff and Britta have just agreed on friendship terms
jokes.punchline: Jeff references Shirley's sex-dream gossip indirectly — a smug, self-satisfied reference to information he wasn't supposed to know
jokes.explanation: Jeff's callback to the sex dream via the casual 'if I'm occasionally naked in your dreams' is smooth and self-serving — classic Jeff smugness in a good way. The indirection is well-chosen. It pays off Shirley's bomb without Jeff explicitly revealing his source.

jokes.text: Britta confronts Shirley: 'Some worries, man. Some worries.' — after Vaughn says 'No worries, man' to Jeff
jokes.setup: Vaughn forgives Jeff with his habitual 'No worries, man'
jokes.punchline: Britta corrects the sentiment — 'some worries' — with flat, accurate precision
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback punchline — 'some worries, man' is a great inversion of Vaughn's signature phrase. It's accurate (there ARE some worries, given everything that just happened), delivered deadpan, and very quotable. Economy is essentially perfect.

jokes.text: Pierce reacts to Vaughn playing guitar and singing in the quad: 'Shirley would have said something funny about that guy.'
jokes.setup: Pierce watches Vaughn perform spontaneously in the quad
jokes.punchline: Pierce — who has spent the episode gossiping — characterizes the absent Shirley as the gossip, while apparently being oblivious to his own behavior
jokes.explanation: Pierce's projection of Shirley as the gossip while being completely unself-aware is good character comedy. His observation that he WISHED Shirley were there to mock Vaughn — while not doing it himself because he doesn't realize he is — is a nice ironic beat.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'You see, Jeff, there are certain things man was not meant to hear... The people we love talk to us in this range.' — a sincere speech about the limits of the Ear-Noculars he just said he'd gotten rid of
jokes.setup: Jeff desperately asks Pierce to lend him the Ear-Noculars to hear what Britta's hearing
jokes.punchline: Pierce delivers a surprisingly sincere wisdom speech about not needing to hear beyond what's meant for you — which is immediately undercut by whatever Jeff hears anyway from across the quad
jokes.explanation: Pierce's unexpected moment of wisdom (filtered through his usual absurdist self-regard) is a good character beat. The gap between his gadget obsession and his sudden philosophical depth is funny. The speech being about hearing 'the people we love' as a dig at Jeff's obsession with Britta works.

jokes.text: Pierce's impression montage: doing impressions of a stoner, Saddam Hussein, a Jamaican man, 'a desperate housewife,' and 'Dr. Doogie Seacrest' (a 40-year-old who thinks he's better than everyone)
jokes.setup: Pierce is performing impressions to entertain himself (and possibly Jeff and others) in the quad
jokes.punchline: The impressions are specific and odd — 'Doogie Seacrest' mashing Ryan Seacrest and Doogie Howser, combined with self-referential age anxiety ('I think I'm better than everyone because I'm 40') is Pierce doing comedy that reveals his own insecurities through the persona
jokes.explanation: 'Dr. Doogie Seacrest' is an inventive coinage — the mashup captures the type of person Pierce resents (young, successful, media-adjacent). The '40-year-old who thinks he's better than everyone' as the persona's defining trait is good because Pierce IS that (but older). The montage structure makes this hard to score as a single joke — it's really several mini-bits in sequence.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I'm not 40. I can hear you through the window, morons.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has been doing impressions including 'Dr. Doogie Seacrest: I'm 40 and I think I'm better than everyone'
jokes.punchline: Pierce breaks the fourth wall of his own impressions to correct the implied age in the character — revealing he's heard their reactions and that his window-hearing is better than the Ear-Noculars were
jokes.explanation: A great button joke. 'I'm not 40' as a defensive interjection — protesting the age in his own character — is funny because it reveals Pierce's age sensitivity while also demonstrating he's been listening all along. 'I can hear you through the window, morons' is a perfect deadpan kicker that makes the Ear-Noculars subplot entirely circular: he never needed them. High character integration, good economy.

jokes.text: Final beat: someone says 'Just pretend like you're asleep.' Then presumably does exactly that.
jokes.setup: Pierce has just caught everyone through the window; there's nowhere to escape
jokes.punchline: The advice to 'just pretend like you're asleep' as a solution to being caught in the act of mocking someone through a window is an absurdist non-solution
jokes.explanation: A quick, silly episode button. The advice is absurd but not especially inventive. Functions as a tag rather than a strong ending joke. Adequate.

tmdb_overview: As Annie recruits Abed and Troy for a psychology class experiment, Jeff and Shirley bond over their mutual fondness for gossip.
insight: Pierce's casual racism hits hardest here: character comedy drives 38 of 66 jokes.
